## Diagnosis

I verified the checkout first: it is byte-identical (modulo CRLF) to upstream `pallets/click` `main` at 8.5.0.dev, and the full suite passes (1882 passed, 95 skipped). There is no injected bug — the "rejection" is Click's intended behavior, so I traced exactly where and how values get rejected in this codebase.

There are two independent rejection layers, and they raise two different exceptions.

**1. Parser layer — an option that is a flag rejects any value**

Whether an option may carry a value is decided at registration time, not at parse time. [`Option.add_to_parser`](C:/Users/91991/.codex/phase16-live/click/src/click/core.py:3296) picks `store`/`append` for value-taking options, but `store_const`/`append_const`/`count` for flags. The internal `_Option.takes_value` in [parser.py](C:/Users/91991/.codex/phase16-live/click/src/click/parser.py:157) is only true for `store`/`append`. When a flag receives `--verbose=yes`, [`_match_long_opt`](C:/Users/91991/.codex/phase16-live/click/src/click/parser.py:382) raises `BadOptionUsage("Option '--verbose' does not take a value.")`. Conversely, a value-taking option with no value available raises `BadOptionUsage("Option '--name' requires an argument.")` in [`_get_value_from_state`](C:/Users/91991/.codex/phase16-live/click/src/click/parser.py:445).

Whether an option is flag-shaped comes from [`Option._infer_flag_kind`](C:/Users/91991/.codex/phase16-live/click/src/click/core.py:3055): `is_flag=True`, a `flag_value`, secondary decls like `--shallow/--deep`, or `count=True` all make it a flag, and `prompt` with `prompt_required=False` sets `_flag_needs_value`, which instead leaves the value unset and falls back to prompting rather than rejecting.

**2. Parameter-type layer — the type rejects the value**

After parsing, [`Parameter.handle_parse_result`](C:/Users/91991/.codex/phase16-live/click/src/click/core.py:2730) → [`type_cast_value`](C:/Users/91991/.codex/phase16-live/click/src/click/core.py:2529) calls `self.type(value, param=self, ctx=ctx)`. Every `ParamType` rejects bad input via [`ParamType.fail`](C:/Users/91991/.codex/phase16-live/click/src/click/types.py:204), which raises `BadParameter`. Reproduced against this checkout:

```
--count 20  → Error: Invalid value for '--count': 20 is not in the range 1<=x<=10.
--count abc → Error: Invalid value for '--count': 'abc' is not a valid integer range.
```

Both come from `IntRange`/`IntParamType` conversion; exit code is 2 in every case.

**Exception handling**

`BadOptionUsage` and `BadParameter` both extend `UsageError` → `ClickException` (`exit_code = 2` in [exceptions.py](C:/Users/91991/.codex/phase16-live/click/src/click/exceptions.py:77)). [`Command.main`](C:/Users/91991/.codex/phase16-live/click/src/click/core.py:1566) catches `ClickException`, prints the usage + `Error: ...` via `e.show()`, and exits with `e.exit_code` (2). In `CliRunner.invoke` that surfaces as `result.exit_code == 2` with `result.exception` being the `SystemExit`, since `main` converts the typed exception before it can escape.

Concrete takeaway: if a command rejects an option value with "does not take a value", the option was declared flag-shaped (`is_flag`/`flag_value`/secondary-opts/count) and the parser never sees a value; if the message is "Invalid value for '--x': ...", parsing succeeded and the rejection came from the option's `ParamType.convert()` via `ParamType.fail` → `BadParameter`. Verified end-to-end against this checkout's `src/click`. Here's the concrete answer.

## How shell completion is added

Completion is wired per-parameter, in two ways:

1. A `shell_complete` callback on the option/argument, signature `(ctx, param, incomplete) -> list[str | CompletionItem]`. Strings are a shortcut for `CompletionItem(value)`; use `CompletionItem(value, help=...)` to give shells help text. This is exactly what `examples/completion/completion.py` does: `show-env` completes argument values via `get_env_vars`, and `select-user` uses `list_users` returning `CompletionItem`s with help strings.
2. Override `shell_complete()` on a custom `ParamType` subclass for type-level completion.

Command names, subcommand names, option names (after a dash), and `Choice`/`Path`/`File` values complete automatically; hidden options/commands are excluded.

## How it's exposed to users

Completion only activates when the CLI is invoked through an installed entry point (not `python`/`python -m`), so it must be registered as a console script — `examples/completion/pyproject.toml` does `[project.scripts] completion = "completion:cli"`.

Users then enable it per shell via the `_<PROG>_COMPLETE=<shell>_source` env var, where `<PROG>` is the executable name uppercased with dashes replaced by underscores. For the example app, `_COMPLETION_COMPLETE`:

- Bash: `eval "$(_COMPLETION_COMPLETE=bash_source completion)"` in `~/.bashrc`
- Zsh: `eval "$(_COMPLETION_COMPLETE=zsh_source completion)"` in `~/.zshrc`
- Fish: `_COMPLETION_COMPLETE=fish_source completion | source` in `~/.config/fish/completions/completion.fish`
- PowerShell: `$env:_COMPLETION_COMPLETE = 'powershell_source'; completion | Out-String | Invoke-Expression; Remove-Item Env:_COMPLETION_COMPLETE` in `$PROFILE`

Optionally pre-generate the script to a file (`... > ~/.foo-bar-complete.bash`) and source that instead of eval. All of this user-facing guidance lives in `docs/shell-completion.md` ("Enabling Completion" section), so the README snippet for a new app should be adapted from there.

## Verification (read-only)

I ran the checkout's own completion machinery: with `_COMPLETION_COMPLETE=bash_complete` and `COMP_WORDS="completion show-env "`, the source tree's Click emitted `plain,<ENV_VAR>...` items — i.e. the `shell_complete=get_env_vars` callback fired correctly for a partial value. (The `bash_source` script-generation mode couldn't be exercised here because this Windows host's `bash --version` output is GBK-encoded, which Click's UTF-8 decoder rejects — a local environment artifact, not a repo issue.) No files were modified.

Debugging done, repo untouched. Here's the concrete diagnosis, reproduced against this 0.52.1 checkout.

## Where the failure actually happens

All lifespan failures surface in one place: [uvicorn/lifespan/on.py:78](/C:/Users/91991/Documents/idea/codex-project-context/benchmarks/workspaces/uvicorn/uvicorn/lifespan/on.py:78). `LifespanOn.main()` runs the app's lifespan protocol and catches `BaseException`, sets `error_occurred = True`, then in `finally` sets both `startup_event` and `shutdown_event` so the server never deadlocks. The severity then depends on the `--lifespan` mode, decided at [uvicorn/lifespan/on.py:58](/C:/Users/91991/Documents/idea/codex-project-context/benchmarks/workspaces/uvicorn/uvicorn/lifespan/on.py:58):

- `--lifespan auto` (default): an exception during startup is downgraded to an INFO log "ASGI 'lifespan' protocol appears unsupported." and the server starts anyway. I reproduced this: app raised `RuntimeError` in lifespan, server still bound the port and served requests, with `should_exit=False`.
- `--lifespan on`: the same exception is logged at ERROR with a full traceback, then "Application startup failed. Exiting." and the process exits with code 3 (`STARTUP_FAILURE`) via [uvicorn/server.py:109](/C:/Users/91991/Documents/idea/codex-project-context/benchmarks/workspaces/uvicorn/uvicorn/server.py:109).

The protocol-level failure (app sends `lifespan.startup.failed`) is different: [uvicorn/lifespan/on.py:102](/C:/Users/91991/Documents/idea/codex-project-context/benchmarks/workspaces/uvicorn/uvicorn/lifespan/on.py:102) sets `startup_failed=True` and logs the message the app provided, which then triggers exit code 3 in both `auto` and `on` modes. Shutdown failures work the same way in reverse (`shutdown_failed`), but by then the server is already exiting.

The most common real-world failure is the auto-mode silent swallow: your app thinks startup succeeded, but its startup code never ran. Diagnostic tell: the log shows "ASGI 'lifespan' protocol appears unsupported." right before "Application startup complete."

## Event-loop behavior during startup/shutdown

The loop is chosen by the loop factory, not created ad hoc: [uvicorn/server.py:77](/C:/Users/91991/Documents/idea/codex-project-context/benchmarks/workspaces/uvicorn/uvicorn/server.py:77) passes `config.get_loop_factory()` into `asyncio_run`, which on this Python 3.11 uses `asyncio.Runner(loop_factory=...)` ([uvicorn/_compat.py:21](/C:/Users/91991/Documents/idea/codex-project-context/benchmarks/workspaces/uvicorn/uvicorn/_compat.py:21)). On Windows that factory yields `ProactorEventLoop` in single-process mode and `SelectorEventLoop` with reload/workers ([uvicorn/loops/asyncio.py](/C:/Users/91991/Documents/idea/codex-project-context/benchmarks/workspaces/uvicorn/uvicorn/loops/asyncio.py:8)).

Two concrete consequences, both reproduced:

- The lifespan coroutine runs on that factory-created loop as a sibling task created in `startup()` at [uvicorn/lifespan/on.py:51](/C:/Users/91991/Documents/idea/codex-project-context/benchmarks/workspaces/uvicorn/uvicorn/lifespan/on.py:51). I confirmed `asyncio.get_running_loop()` inside lifespan returned the `ProactorEventLoop` created by the `--loop asyncio` factory. The `startup_event`/`shutdown_event`/`receive_queue` primitives are constructed loop-free in `__init__` and bind lazily on first await, so they can't cross loops here.
- Calling `asyncio.run()` inside `lifespan.startup` raises "asyncio.run() cannot be called from a running event loop" — swallowed in `auto` mode, fatal exit code 3 in `on` mode. This is the classic misdiagnosis: the traceback gets attributed to "Exception in 'lifespan' protocol" at [uvicorn/lifespan/on.py:96](/C:/Users/91991/Documents/idea/codex-project-context/benchmarks/workspaces/uvicorn/uvicorn/lifespan/on.py:96).

One genuine gap in the shutdown path: `timeout_graceful_shutdown` bounds only the connection/task draining at [uvicorn/server.py:288](/C:/Users/91991/Documents/idea/codex-project-context/benchmarks/workspaces/uvicorn/uvicorn/server.py:288); the subsequent `lifespan.shutdown()` wait at [uvicorn/server.py:302](/C:/Users/91991/Documents/idea/codex-project-context/benchmarks/workspaces/uvicorn/uvicorn/server.py:302) awaits [uvicorn/lifespan/on.py:70](/C:/Users/91991/Documents/idea/codex-project-context/benchmarks/workspaces/uvicorn/uvicorn/lifespan/on.py:70) with no timeout, so an app that never answers `lifespan.shutdown` hangs the process indefinitely — only a second Ctrl+C (`force_exit`) skips lifespan shutdown entirely.

## Bottom line

If you see exit code 3 or "Application startup failed. Exiting.", your lifespan startup broke and uvicorn refused to boot (or silently skipped it in `auto` mode — rerun with `--lifespan on` to surface the traceback). If shutdown hangs, the app isn't answering `lifespan.shutdown`, and uvicorn won't force it without a second signal.

Verification: `tests/test_lifespan.py` 16 passed, `tests/test_server.py` 11 passed/4 skipped; four in-process reproductions captured the exact log lines and exit codes above. `files changed: 0` — nothing was modified.

**This checkout is a uvicorn fork with a third HTTP protocol, `zttp`, already registered but never auto-selected.** Switching to it requires an explicit setting plus a compatible runtime.

**How to make the change (three equivalent entry points)**

- CLI: `uvicorn main:app --http zttp`
- Env var: `UVICORN_HTTP=zttp` (click's `auto_envvar_prefix="UVICORN"` in [main.py](/C:/Users/91991/.codex/phase16-live/uvicorn/uvicorn/main.py:61))
- Programmatic: `uvicorn.run("main:app", http="zttp")`, or pass the class directly: `http=uvicorn.protocols.http.zttp_impl.ZttpProtocol` (Config accepts a protocol class or string).

The registry already maps `"zttp"` to `uvicorn.protocols.http.zttp_impl:ZttpProtocol` in [config.py](/C:/Users/91991/.codex/phase16-live/uvicorn/uvicorn/config.py:55), so no code change is needed to select it.

**Two conditions that would otherwise break request handling**

1. `zttp` must be importable. `--http auto` only chooses httptools (falling back to h11); it never picks zttp, and an explicit `--http zttp` with the package missing fails hard: `Config.load()`'s `import_from_string` logs an error and exits with `STARTUP_FAILURE` (3) — no silent fallback. The package is pinned at `zttp==0.0.20` with a `python_version >= '3.12'` marker ([pyproject.toml](/C:/Users/91991/.codex/phase16-live/uvicorn/pyproject.toml:73)), and it lives in the dev dependency group, not the `standard` extra, so production installs must add `zttp==0.0.20` explicitly. This machine runs Python 3.11.15 without zttp, so the switch only works on a ≥3.12 interpreter with the package installed.
2. Keep the generic server settings at their defaults — `timeout_keep_alive=5`, `limit_concurrency=None`, `backlog=2048`, `limit_max_requests`, `server_header`/`date_header` — they all flow through `ServerState`/`FlowControl` identically for every protocol. `--h11-max-incomplete-event-size` is h11-only and simply has no effect under zttp. Keep `ws` on `auto`: `ZttpProtocol.handle_websocket_upgrade` replays the buffered upgrade request into the selected WS protocol and swaps the transport protocol, so WebSocket apps keep working.

**Why request handling survives the switch**

[zttp_impl.py](/C:/Users/91991/.codex/phase16-live/uvicorn/uvicorn/protocols/http/zttp_impl.py:28) normalizes response framing where zttp is stricter: it strips `Transfer-Encoding` on 1xx/204, drops `Content-Length` when `Transfer-Encoding` is present, auto-adds `transfer-encoding: chunked` when the app supplies neither, enforces Content-Length accounting, sends `100 Continue`, and handles keep-alive/close, 400 on parse errors, and 500 on ASGI exceptions. The existing suite already runs every HTTP/WebSocket/middleware test against httptools, h11, and zttp via the `http_protocol_cls` fixture ([conftest.py](/C:/Users/91991/.codex/phase16-live/uvicorn/tests/conftest.py:258)), so verification is `pytest tests/protocols/test_http.py tests/protocols/test_websocket.py` on Python ≥3.12 with zttp installed.

I traced the abort paths in the checkout (axios v1.19.0, clean at `ba98559`). The short answer: Axios has two separate abort code paths, and only one of them produces a cancellation error — plus it discards the reason you pass to `AbortController.abort()`.

## Why it looks like a generic failure

**Path 1 — Axios's own cancellation plumbing** (CancelToken subscription or the `abort` listener Axios attaches to your signal) rejects with a `CanceledError`: name `CanceledError`, code `ERR_CANCELED`, and `__CANCEL__: true`, so `axios.isCancel(err)` is true ([CanceledError.js](C:/Users/91991/Documents/idea/codex-project-context/benchmarks/workspaces/axios/lib/cancel/CanceledError.js:14), [isCancel.js](C:/Users/91991/Documents/idea/codex-project-context/benchmarks/workspaces/axios/lib/cancel/isCancel.js:3)).

**Path 2 — transport-level aborts that bypass that plumbing** reject with a plain `AxiosError` that is *not* a cancellation:

- Browser XHR: `request.onabort` and the `onloadend` status-0 branch both reject `new AxiosError('Request aborted', ECONNABORTED)` ([xhr.js:62](C:/Users/91991/Documents/idea/codex-project-context/benchmarks/workspaces/axios/lib/adapters/xhr.js:62), [xhr.js:135](C:/Users/91991/Documents/idea/codex-project-context/benchmarks/workspaces/axios/lib/adapters/xhr.js:135)). The comment there is explicit: "browser request cancellation (as opposed to a manual cancellation)".
- Node http: if the socket dies independently of the abort emitter, `req.on('error')` wraps the native error via `AxiosError.from` ([http.js:1256](C:/Users/91991/Documents/idea/codex-project-context/benchmarks/workspaces/axios/lib/adapters/http.js:1256)), so you get `code: 'ECONNRESET'`, message `'socket hang up'`, and — because `AxiosError.from` copies the native error's `name` ([AxiosError.js:79](C:/Users/91991/Documents/idea/codex-project-context/benchmarks/workspaces/axios/lib/core/AxiosError.js:79)) — the error presents as a generic `Error`, with `isCancel(err) === false`. A mid-body stream abort is `ERR_BAD_RESPONSE` ("stream has been aborted", [http.js:1206](C:/Users/91991/Documents/idea/codex-project-context/benchmarks/workspaces/axios/lib/adapters/http.js:1206)).

**Second genericness problem — the abort reason is dropped.** `signal.addEventListener('abort', handler)` delivers an `Event` (verified live: `type: 'abort'`), not the reason; the reason lives on `signal.reason`. Both the XHR and http adapters check `cancel.type` / `reason.type` and, since it's truthy, always construct a stock `CanceledError(null, ...)` with the default message `"canceled"` ([xhr.js:221](C:/Users/91991/Documents/idea/codex-project-context/benchmarks/workspaces/axios/lib/adapters/xhr.js:221), [http.js:583](C:/Users/91991/Documents/idea/codex-project-context/benchmarks/workspaces/axios/lib/adapters/http.js:583)). So `controller.abort(new Error('user clicked cancel'))` surfaces as `CanceledError: canceled` in those adapters — your reason never reaches the catch block. CancelToken does preserve a custom message (it passes its own `CanceledError` through `subscribe`), and the fetch adapter is the one that properly re-throws `composedSignal.reason` ([fetch.js:556](C:/Users/91991/Documents/idea/codex-project-context/benchmarks/workspaces/axios/lib/adapters/fetch.js:556)).

## How to tell them apart

- `axios.isCancel(err)` (equivalently `err instanceof axios.CanceledError` or `err.code === 'ERR_CANCELED'`) — deliberate cancellation via AbortController/CancelToken. This is the only reliable "user asked to cancel" signal.
- `err.code === 'ECONNABORTED'` without `isCancel` — transport-level abort (browser/XHR aborted, status-0 response), *not* a recognized user cancellation. Note it's also the legacy timeout code unless `transitional.clarifyTimeoutError` is set, which upgrades timeouts to `ETIMEDOUT`.
- Node `ECONNRESET` / `'socket hang up'`, or `ERR_BAD_RESPONSE` "stream has been aborted" — the connection/response was torn down at the transport level; again `isCancel` is false.

Practical takeaway: check `axios.isCancel(err)` before treating anything else as a network failure, and if you need the original abort reason on the XHR/http adapters, read it from your own `signal.reason` (Axios won't surface it for you there).

This repo is the Ruff source tree itself (v0.16.2), so the answer is grounded in its actual configuration and resolution code. Read-only investigation; nothing was modified.

## Quick answer

The canonical debugging command is `ruff check <file> --show-settings`, which prints the fully resolved settings (including which config file was used, the exact enabled rule set, and per-file-ignore globs). Then isolate with `--isolated --select <RULE>` to tell "config suppressed it" from "rule doesn't fire on this code."

## Diagnostic sequence

1. **Is the file even linted?** `ruff check --show-files <path>` prints the files Ruff would check under current settings (implemented in [args.rs](/C:/Users/91991/.codex/phase16-live/ruff/crates/ruff/src/args.rs:505)). If your file is missing, it's caught by `exclude`/`extend-exclude`, `.gitignore` (`respect-gitignore`), `force-exclude`, or isn't a recognized Python/TOML file type.

2. **What settings apply?** `ruff check <file> --show-settings` resolves settings for that file and prints the config path plus the full `Settings` struct — notably `linter.rules.enabled` (the exact effective rule set), `linter.rules.should_fix`, `linter.per_file_ignores`, `linter.per_file_target_version`, and `linter.preview` (see the display fields in [settings/mod.rs](/C:/Users/91991/.codex/phase16-live/ruff/crates/ruff_linter/src/settings/mod.rs:284) and the command in [show_settings.rs](/C:/Users/91991/.codex/phase16-live/ruff/crates/ruff/src/commands/show_settings.rs:39)). Note it prints the global table plus the per-file globs — you match your file's path against the globs yourself, since per-file ignores are applied per-file at lint time, not folded into the displayed table.

3. **Is the rule itself applicable?** `ruff rule <CODE>` shows whether the rule is stable, preview-only, deprecated/removed, or redirected (e.g., `U007` → `UP007`). Unknown codes in `select` are silently ignored, so a typo or redirect can quietly enable nothing.

4. **Does the rule fire at all without your config?** `ruff check --isolated --select <CODE> <file>` (add `--preview` for preview rules) bypasses config files and `.gitignore`. If it fires isolated but not normally, the cause is in config; if it never fires, the rule doesn't match your code (or is gated by Python version).

## Common root causes, with this repo's source as evidence

- **Not selected.** Ruff 0.16.0 expanded the default rule set from 59 to 413 rules but also removed 18 pycodestyle/pyflakes rules from defaults (`E401`, `E402`, `E741`, `F403`, `F405`, etc.) — see [CHANGELOG.md](/C:/Users/91991/.codex/phase16-live/ruff/CHANGELOG.md:92). If the rule you expect isn't in `select`/`extend-select` and isn't in `DEFAULT_SELECTORS` ([settings/mod.rs](/C:/Users/91991/.codex/phase16-live/ruff/crates/ruff_linter/src/settings/mod.rs:357)), it's off.
- **Ignored.** `ignore`/`extend-ignore` or a matching `lint.per-file-ignores` glob. Per-file ignores can only *disable* rules: at lint time `LintContext::new` clones the rule table and disables any rule whose per-file-ignore glob matches the path ([checkers/ast/mod.rs](/C:/Users/91991/.codex/phase16-live/ruff/crates/ruff_linter/src/checkers/ast/mod.rs:3434)).
- **Preview gating.** Preview rules are excluded from prefix selectors unless `preview = true`/`--preview`, and `explicit-preview-rules` requires naming codes exactly ([rule_selector.rs](/C:/Users/91991/.codex/phase16-live/ruff/crates/ruff_linter/src/rule_selector.rs:281)).
- **Python-version gating.** Many rules require a minimum `target-version`; e.g., UP007 (`Optional[X]` → `X | None`) only applies at ≥3.10 ([use_pep604_annotation.rs](/C:/Users/91991/.codex/phase16-live/ruff/crates/ruff_linter/src/rules/pyupgrade/rules/use_pep604_annotation.rs:174)). `per-file-target-version` can override this per path ([settings/mod.rs](/C:/Users/91991/.codex/phase16-live/ruff/crates/ruff_linter/src/settings/mod.rs:885)). This repo itself is a live example: [pyproject.toml](/C:/Users/91991/.codex/phase16-live/ruff/pyproject.toml:71) sets `target-version = "py38"` while selecting `UP`, so UP007 etc. can never fire here.
- **Inline suppressions.** A bare `# ruff: noqa` at the top of the file disables everything in it; an uncoded `# noqa` on a line disables everything on that line; 0.16 also added line-level `# ruff: ignore[CODE]`. `RUF100` flags unused noqas if enabled.
- **Convention-driven disabling.** `[lint.pydocstyle] convention = "..."` silently disables all `D` rules outside that convention (documented in [docs/faq.md](/C:/Users/91991/.codex/phase16-live/ruff/docs/faq.md:470)).
- **File kind.** Some rules only apply to certain source types (e.g., `PYI` rules on `.pyi` stubs); confirm with `--extension` mappings if the extension is unusual.
- **It fires but doesn't fix.** `fixable`/`unfixable`, `--fix` not passed, or the fix is preview/unsafe (`--unsafe-fixes`).

## One-liner triage

```
ruff check <file> --show-files          # is it linted at all?
ruff check <file> --show-settings       # resolved rules + per-file ignores
ruff rule <CODE>                        # preview? redirected? removed?
ruff check --isolated --select <CODE> <file>   # does the rule work without your config?
```

The most frequent real-world answers are: the rule isn't in the enabled set (especially after the 0.16 default-set change), a `per-file-ignores` glob matches the file, or the rule is version-gated by `target-version`/`per-file-target-version`.

I've traced the full timeout path in this repo (httpx 0.28.1 source at `C:\Users\91991\.codex\phase16-live\httpx`) and reproduced it live against a local stalling server. No files were modified.

## What happens when the request times out

The timeout is enforced by `httpcore` at the socket level. It raises `httpcore.ReadTimeout`/`ConnectTimeout`/`WriteTimeout`/`PoolTimeout`, and httpx's transport re-maps those to its own exception classes in [default.py](C:\Users\91991\.codex\phase16-live\httpx\httpx\_transports\default.py:74). So user code catches `httpx.TimeoutException` (base of all four) or a specific subclass, and the exception carries a `.request` attribute for debugging which URL/phase failed. My live repro confirmed the chain: a server that accepts the request but never answers raised `httpx.ReadTimeout` after ~0.5s, and the traceback showed the `httpcore.ConnectTimeout → httpx.ConnectTimeout` mapping.

## How timeouts are configured

There are four independent phases, defined in the `Timeout` class in [_config.py](C:\Users\91991\.codex\phase16-live\httpx\httpx\_config.py:72): `connect`, `read`, `write`, `pool`. The library default is `Timeout(timeout=5.0)` (line 246), i.e. 5s for all four phases.

Client-level: `httpx.Client(timeout=10.0)` sets a default applied to every request. When you omit `timeout` on a request, the `USE_CLIENT_DEFAULT` sentinel in [_client.py](C:\Users\91991\.codex\phase16-live\httpx\httpx\_client.py:104) tells `build_request`/`_set_timeout` to copy the client's config into `request.extensions["timeout"]` ([_client.py:377](C:\Users\91991\.codex\phase16-live\httpx\httpx\_client.py:377), [_client.py:583](C:\Users\91991\.codex\phase16-live\httpx\httpx\_client.py:583)).

Per-request: `client.get(url, timeout=0.5)` overrides the client default for that single request only. Crucially, `timeout=None` is not "use the default" — it explicitly disables timeouts, overriding the client config.

Live verification of the precedence: a client created with `timeout=30.0` still raised `ReadTimeout` after 0.52s when the request passed `timeout=0.5`. And `build_request` inspection showed exactly what lands in the request: client default → `{connect: 10.0, read: 10.0, write: 10.0, pool: 10.0}`; per-request `0.25` → all phases 0.25; explicit `None` → all phases `None`. Per-phase config works as `httpx.Timeout(10.0, connect=2.0, read=None)` → `{connect: 2.0, read: None, write: 10.0, pool: 10.0}`.

So the likely bug in a timeout-raising request is either: the endpoint is genuinely slower than the 5s default (fix with a larger client-level or per-request timeout), a per-request `timeout=` is overriding a generous client default, or `timeout=None` accidentally disabled the protection. To debug: catch `httpx.TimeoutException`, read `exc.request.url` and the exception subclass — `ReadTimeout` means the server responded slowly, `ConnectTimeout` means the connection wasn't established in time, and `PoolTimeout` means it couldn't acquire a pooled connection.

## Verdict

The checkout is a byte-identical snapshot of upstream Catch2 devel tip `0aeb8185` (v3.15.3-dev, stamped 2026-08-11/12) — nothing is locally patched. I built the full SelfTest suite with MSVC 19.44 and ran the approval harness: all baselines pass, so the console/XML/TAP/TeamCity/sonarqube/compact reporters' per-section output is intact. The missing per-section diagnostics are real upstream gaps in two reporters, reproduced below with a probe binary.

## Where per-section logging actually exists

Console and XML are fine. A failing assertion inside a section prints the section chain and its in-scope INFO messages ([catch_reporter_console.cpp](/C:/Users/91991/.codex/phase16-live/catch2/src/catch2/reporters/catch_reporter_console.cpp:564)); `-s` additionally logs passing sections with their messages, and `-w NoAssertions` prints `No assertions in section '...'` ([catch_reporter_console.cpp](/C:/Users/91991/.codex/phase16-live/catch2/src/catch2/reporters/catch_reporter_console.cpp:446)). Scoped-logging semantics are documented in [logging.md](/C:/Users/91991/.codex/phase16-live/catch2/docs/logging.md:6): `INFO`/`CAPTURE` messages attach to assertions in their scope and only print on failure (or with `-s`), `UNSCOPED_INFO` is cleared by the next assertion/section/test case.

## Where it's missing (reproduced)

JUnit drops assertion-free sections entirely. The `<testcase>` element is only written when a section has assertions or captured std output ([catch_reporter_junit.cpp](/C:/Users/91991/.codex/phase16-live/catch2/src/catch2/reporters/catch_reporter_junit.cpp:202)):

```cpp
if ( sectionNode.stats.assertions.total() > 0
   || !sectionNode.stdOut.empty()
   || !sectionNode.stdErr.empty() ) {
    xml.scopedElement( "testcase" );
```

A probe test with three sections produced JUnit `<testcase>` nodes for the failing and passing sections but none for the `assertion-free section`, even though it executed — and the suite `tests="2"` attribute counts assertions ([catch_reporter_junit.cpp](/C:/Users/91991/.codex/phase16-live/catch2/src/catch2/reporters/catch_reporter_junit.cpp:139)), so it disagrees with the emitted node count. Console, by contrast, logs that section. This matches open upstream PR #3187 ("Fix JUnit output for assertion-free test cases"), which is not merged at this commit.

JSON drops all assertion diagnostics. Sections are logged as nested `path` nodes, but each assertion emits only `kind`/`source-location`/`status` — the failure message, INFO, and expansion text are all swallowed by the `// TODO: messages` placeholder in [catch_reporter_json.cpp](/C:/Users/91991/.codex/phase16-live/catch2/src/catch2/reporters/catch_reporter_json.cpp:304) (with a similar metadata TODO at line 280). A failing `CHECK(1 == 2)` appears in JSON as just `"status": false` with no message.

One related gotcha from the recent "per-reporter verbosity" change: console/compact/XML decide whether to show successful results via the global config's `includeSuccessfulResults()` (set only by `-s`), not the new per-reporter verbosity, so `-r console::verbosity=high` alone does not add `-s`-style per-section logging.

## FAQ: global setup and cleanup

Per [docs/faq.md](/C:/Users/91991/.codex/phase16-live/catch2/docs/faq.md:16):

- Global setup/teardown that should run only when tests will actually run: write a custom event listener and put the code in the `testRun*` events (e.g. `testRunStarting`/`testRunEnded`).
- Cleaning up global state between tests: write a custom event listener and put the cleanup in `testCase*` events (per test case) or `testCasePartial*` events (per partial run, e.g. under sharding), depending on how often cleanup must happen.

The hooks exist on `IEventListener` in [catch_interfaces_reporter.hpp](/C:/Users/91991/.codex/phase16-live/catch2/src/catch2/interfaces/catch_interfaces_reporter.hpp:170).

tasks.final_answer:
I have everything needed from the checkout's docs and code. No files were modified (`files changed: 0`).

## What's actually needed

Both features are built into uvicorn already; "adding" them to a deployment means dependency + configuration changes, not code changes.

**1. WebSocket support.** It activates automatically but only if a WS backend package is installed. The default `ws="auto"` ([auto.py](/C:/Users/91991/.codex/phase16-live/uvicorn/uvicorn/protocols/websockets/auto.py)) resolves as: `websockets` installed → `websockets-sansio` protocol; otherwise `wsproto` → legacy protocol; with neither, WebSockets are disabled. So the deployment must install `pip install "uvicorn[standard]"` (brings `websockets`, `httptools`, `uvloop`, PyYAML) and should pin the implementation explicitly with `--ws websockets-sansio`. Relevant tuning flags with defaults: `--ws-ping-interval 20`, `--ws-ping-timeout 20`, `--ws-max-size 16777216`, `--ws-max-queue 32`, `--ws-per-message-deflate` (on). If this deployment sits behind Nginx, the proxy must forward `Upgrade`/`Connection` headers (the docs show the exact `map $http_upgrade` + `proxy_set_header` block).

**2. Request logging.** Per-request lines come from the `uvicorn.access` logger, which is on by default (`access_log=True`). Make it explicit with `--access-log --log-level info`. For timestamped/structured access lines, ship a log config and pass `--log-config log_config.yaml` (YAML needs PyYAML, i.e. `uvicorn[standard]`); the access formatter must extend `uvicorn.logging.AccessFormatter` to keep the `%(client_addr)s`, `%(request_line)s`, `%(status_code)s` placeholders ([logging.md](/C:/Users/91991/.codex/phase16-live/uvicorn/docs/concepts/logging.md)). Use `--no-access-log` only if you want it off.

## Concrete deployment change

```bash
pip install "uvicorn[standard]"
uvicorn main:app --host 0.0.0.0 --port 8000 \
  --ws websockets-sansio --ws-ping-interval 20 --ws-ping-timeout 20 \
  --access-log --log-level info --log-config log_config.yaml
```

Programmatic equivalent:

```python
uvicorn.run("main:app", host="0.0.0.0", port=8000, ws="websockets-sansio",
            access_log=True, log_level="info", log_config="log_config.yaml")
```

For a Docker deployment, the [docker.md](/C:/Users/91991/.codex/phase16-live/uvicorn/docs/deployment/docker.md) CMD becomes `["uv", "run", "uvicorn", "main:app", "--host", "0.0.0.0", "--port", "8000", "--ws", "websockets-sansio", "--access-log", "--log-config", "log_config.yaml"]` — and make sure `pyproject.toml` depends on `uvicorn[standard]` plus the `log_config.yaml` is copied into the image. If running under Gunicorn instead, uvicorn flags aren't passed through directly; subclass `UvicornWorker` and set `CONFIG_KWARGS`.

## How to add a new formatter option (e.g. `format.example-option`)

1. **Declare it in the config surface**: add `pub example_option: Option<T>` to [`FormatOptions`](C:/Users/91991/.codex/phase16-live/ruff/crates/ruff_workspace/src/options.rs:3856) with an `#[option(default = …, value_type = …, example = …)]` attribute. This struct is `serde(deny_unknown_fields)` (typos are hard errors — verified by the CLI test at [format.rs](C:/Users/91991/.codex/phase16-live/ruff/crates/ruff/tests/cli/format.rs:1135)) and derives `schemars::JsonSchema`, so the attribute drives both `ruff.schema.json` and the generated settings docs.
2. **Resolve it**: in [`Configuration::resolve_settings`](C:/Users/91991/.codex/phase16-live/ruff/crates/ruff_workspace/src/configuration.rs:236), the `FormatterSettings` literal gets `example_option: format.example_option.unwrap_or(format_defaults.example_option)`, where `format_defaults` comes from `FormatterSettings::default()` — the same fallback chain used by `line_width`, `indent_width`, and `quote_style`.
3. **Carry it in runtime settings**: add the resolved field to [`FormatterSettings`](C:/Users/91991/.codex/phase16-live/ruff/crates/ruff_workspace/src/settings.rs:181) and wire it into the builder chain in `FormatterSettings::to_format_options`.
4. **Consume it in the formatter engine**: add the field, a serde default fn, a getter, and a `with_*` builder to [`PyFormatOptions`](C:/Users/91991/.codex/phase16-live/ruff/crates/ruff_python_formatter/src/options.rs:18), then read it in the formatting logic. If it changes output style (not just plumbing), gate it behind preview with a named helper in [preview.rs](C:/Users/91991/.codex/phase16-live/ruff/crates/ruff_python_formatter/src/preview.rs:1), like `is_fluent_layout_split_first_call_enabled`.
5. **Optional CLI flag**: only a handful of formatter settings are exposed as flags (`--line-length`, `--preview`, `--target-version` on [`FormatCommand`](C:/Users/91991/.codex/phase16-live/ruff/crates/ruff/src/args.rs:524)); if you add one, also map it into `ExplicitConfigOverrides` in `FormatCommand::partition` so it beats config-file values.
6. **Regenerate + test**: `cargo dev generate-json-schema` ([generate_json_schema.rs](C:/Users/91991/.codex/phase16-live/ruff/crates/ruff_dev/src/generate_json_schema.rs:19)) rewrites `ruff.schema.json`; `scripts/generate_mkdocs.py` regenerates docs; update prose in `docs/formatter.md`; add fixtures/snapshots under `crates/ruff_python_formatter/tests/`. The playground (wasm) only needs a change if it should expose the option: [ruff_wasm/src/lib.rs](C:/Users/91991/.codex/phase16-live/ruff/crates/ruff_wasm/src/lib.rs:296), and the LSP's own [`FormatOptions`](C:/Users/91991/.codex/phase16-live/ruff/crates/ruff_server/src/session/options.rs:259) only for server-level flags — normal options reach the server through workspace config resolution.

## How the formatter interacts with the linter

They are architecturally independent: `ruff_linter` has no dependency on `ruff_python_formatter` (verified), and both are resolved side-by-side from one `Configuration` into [`Settings { linter, formatter, … }`](C:/Users/91991/.codex/phase16-live/ruff/crates/ruff_workspace/src/settings.rs:23). Interaction happens in three ways:

- **Shared config keys**: top-level `line-length` feeds both `LinterSettings.line_length` (E501, COM812, …) and `FormatterSettings.line_width` (with the formatter's 88-char default only when unset), and top-level `indent-width`, `target-version`, `exclude`, and the global `preview` fallback are shared the same way.
- **Compatibility warnings at the CLI layer**: `warn_incompatible_formatter_settings` in [commands/format.rs](C:/Users/91991/.codex/phase16-live/ruff/crates/ruff/src/commands/format.rs:1083) (called from both `ruff format` and `ruff format --stdin`) walks every per-file resolved setting and compares `setting.linter` against `setting.formatter`. It warns on COM812/D203 unconditionally; W191 and D206 when `format.indent-style="tab"`; E111/E114 when `indent-width ≠ 4`; Q000/Q001/Q002/Q003 when `flake8-quotes` conflicts with `format.quote-style`; ISC001-off + `allow-multiline=false`; and isort `lines-after-imports`, `lines-between-types`, `force-wrap-aliases`, `split-on-trailing-comma` vs `skip-magic-trailing-comma`. If a new option creates a conflict with lint rules, this function is where it gets detected.
- **Preview coordination**: formatter preview styles are wrapped in named predicates, and some note that stabilizing the formatter style requires stabilizing the corresponding linter preview behavior at the same time (see [preview.rs](C:/Users/91991/.codex/phase16-live/ruff/crates/ruff_python_formatter/src/preview.rs:29)).

So a new option typically touches five crates (`ruff_workspace` twice, `ruff_python_formatter`, optionally `ruff`, and docs/schema generation); the linter only becomes involved if the option can contradict existing lint rules, in which case the check belongs in `warn_incompatible_formatter_settings`.

(Per the project-context skill I queried the Context MCP first; it pointed to the formatter/configuration docs, but the concrete flow above was verified against the Rust sources, with no files modified.)

- Spec grammar: `name::out=<file>::colour-mode=ansi|win32|none|default::verbosity=quiet|normal|high::X<key>=<value>`. Parsed in [catch_reporter_spec_parser.cpp](/C:/Users/91991/.codex/phase16-live/catch2/src/catch2/internal/catch_reporter_spec_parser.cpp:116) (`out`, `colour-mode`, `verbosity` are Catch2-handled; `X`-prefixed keys pass through to the reporter's `customOptions`).
